titulo.texto: Polychrome Jar from Paquimé / Casas Grandes

frase_gancho.texto: Red and black geometry from the great adobe city of the desert.

puente_narrativo.texto: From geometric designs we move on to the human face. Look for a vessel shaped like a seated person, with its body and face covered in red and black lines.

guion_corto.texto: This pot comes from Paquimé, also called Casas Grandes, in Chihuahua. It is about twenty centimeters tall and was made about eight hundred years ago. It has a round body, a cream-colored background, and decoration painted in black and red: bands, stepped triangles, and spirals, all drawn by hand with astonishing precision. Paquimé was one of the largest cities of the north: multistory adobe houses, water brought in through canals, and a huge flow of trade. Turquoise from the southwestern United States, seashells, copper bells, and macaw feathers all arrived here. This pot is a witness to that wealth. Look at how each line joins the next.

guion_largo.texto:
Some cities tell their story in stone, and others tell it in adobe, a material that rain dissolves. That is why Paquimé is a remarkable achievement. Its houses were raised from earth, sometimes several stories high, and walls still stand today. In nineteen ninety-eight, UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site. “Casas Grandes” is the name the Spaniards gave it; Paquimé is how it is known today.

Paquimé had something astonishing in the middle of the desert: running water. It is thought that stone canals brought water from nearby springs to the city and distributed it among the houses, and that there were also drains. In a land where water is the most precious thing, controlling its path gave power. It is no coincidence that the spirals and wavy lines on the ceramics have been linked to water.

Among the most curious finds are pens for scarlet macaws, birds that live in the tropical rainforest, more than a thousand kilometers to the south. The people of Paquimé raised them for their feathers, which were used in ceremonies and traded. Think of the [headdress](mna_s06_penacho_moctezuma) you saw in the Mexica Hall: feathers were a treasure. Here they were raised to have them close at hand.

And now I keep a promise from the Oaxaca Hall. Do you remember the turquoise on the Mixtec skull? It is thought that a good part of what reached Mesoamerica came from the southwestern United States, and that cities like this one were stops along the way. Hundreds of the [copper bells](mna_s10_cobre_purepecha) that you saw in the West Hall have also been found here. Everything traveled: copper went north, turquoise went south, and seashells came from the coast.

Look at the pot again. The stepped triangles may recall the steps of buildings, and the spirals, the wind and the water. In the Southwest and in Mesoamerica, the serpent was associated with rain, like the [Feathered Serpent](mna_s04_templo_quetzalcoatl) you saw in Teotihuacán and Tula, so it is no surprise to find it on desert vessels. We do not know exactly what these designs meant, but we do know that they were repeated, and that they were repeated with rhythm.

A pot like this was used to store grain, water, or food. It was not a display-case object, even if we see it that way today. Painting like this demanded a steady hand: one crooked line ruins the whole band. The potters shaped it by hand, without a wheel, smoothed the surface with stones, and fired it in the open air. It is thought that Paquimé had specialized workshops, and that its ceramics were carried to other peoples.

Around the year 1450, the city was abandoned. It is thought that it was attacked and burned, though it is not known by whom. When the Spaniards reached the region, it was already a city in ruins. But its ceramics, orderly and luminous, still speak of a city that lived by trading with the world.

texto: Follow one of the bands of stepped triangles with your eyes
Find the spirals and compare the red with the black
Notice the cream-colored background and the round shape of the pot

texto.Period: Postclassic / Paquimé Middle Period (peak between 1100 and 1300 AD)
texto.Material: Polychrome clay (red and black paint on cream)

texto.pregunta: Myth: There were never any great cities in the northern desert.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Paquimé had multistory adobe houses, water canals, and trade with places more than a thousand kilometers away. In nineteen ninety-eight UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site.
